item.title: Is Too Much Choice Bad for Love?
item.description:
Relationships

Is Too Much Choice Bad for Love?

The paradox of abundance in modern romance.

Posted October 10, 2026

Key points
  • Romantic abundance facilitates finding a partner but can complicate sustaining enduring love.
  • The availability of alternatives encourages comparison, regret, and lower commitment.
  • Profound love often requires limiting attention to alternative partners.
  • Psychological flexibility can help people navigate romantic abundance without sacrificing commitment.

"In the desert, every thorn is a rose."—A cultural proverb

Our era of romantic abundance appears to increase our chances of falling in love and finding a partner. Yet having too much of a good thing may also make profound, enduring love more difficult. Does romantic abundance enhance the prospects of love, or undermine our ability to sustain it?

Measuring Romantic Value

“There is only one happiness in this life, to love and be loved.”—George Sand

Assessing a person's romantic value involves two major dimensions. The first is a nonrelational dimension, which concerns traits that are valuable in themselves, such as humor, wealth, intelligence, or wisdom. The second is a relational dimension, which concerns suitability, namely, the unique fit between two particular people. The nonrelational dimension is relatively straightforward. Most people agree that intelligence or wealth are desirable. Suitability, however, is far more complex because it depends on personal and situational circumstances that are difficult to predict.

Consider intelligence. It is generally regarded as attractive, but a large intellectual gap between partners may diminish its relational value. Wealth presents a similar case. Although usually considered desirable, wealth may increase access to romantic alternatives, potentially complicating commitment. Even when two people possess many admirable qualities, their relational value may remain low if they fail to bring out the best in one another.

These two dimensions correspond to two central romantic tasks: finding a partner and sustaining a loving relationship. Romantic abundance facilitates the former but may complicate the latter. We encounter more people who possess desirable traits, yet often become less willing to invest deeply in any one relationship. It seems that polyamorous individuals report many of the same challenges as monogamous individuals, while they may have higher sexual satisfaction (Rogier, G. et al., 2024); (Tatum, A. K., et. al., 2026).

The Difficulties of Romantic Abundance

"Sex without love is merely healthy exercise." — Robert A. Heinlein

Source: pexels-cesar-o-neill-26650613-29468350

Romantic abundance creates several challenges in romantic decision-making. Among the most significant are the search for a perfect partner rather than a suitable one, the temptation of the road not taken, the backup strategy, and reduced commitment and investment.

Perfect person vs. suitable partner

Romantic maximizers seek the perfect partner, whereas satisficers focus on finding someone who is sufficiently compatible and capable of fostering a good relationship. Maximizers spend more time comparing their current partner to former partners, potential alternatives, and even other people's partners. They also tend to experience greater regret and engage in more counterfactual thinking. Romantic abundance encourages this maximizing mindset. When alternatives appear endless, it becomes tempting to search indefinitely for the perfect person instead of appreciating a suitable partner.

The temptation of the road not taken

In conditions of romantic abundance, the road not taken can become especially alluring. When alternatives seem readily available, staying in one relationship may feel less like commitment and more like missing out. Modern lovers often find little peace, not necessarily because their current relationship is inadequate, but because another possibility always appears more exciting. Yet chasing imagined possibilities is often part of the problem rather than the solution. Fantasies about what might be "out there" can become a poor substitute for what already exists and may destabilize an otherwise valuable relationship.

The backup strategy

"Save a boyfriend for a rainy day—and another, in case it doesn't rain."—Mae West

Romantic abundance encourages a backup strategy: maintaining potential replacements in case a relationship ends. This tendency is particularly visible on dating platforms, where a seemingly endless stream of prospective partners makes it easy to move on to the next option. When alternatives are plentiful, disappointment may no longer motivate deeper engagement; instead, it encourages continued searching. The availability of replacements can reduce the incentive to invest in a worthwhile relationship and develop greater intimacy. This reflects the romantic principle that more can become less (Ben-Ze'ev, 2019).

Lower commitment and investment

Romantic abundance may also weaken commitment. Commitment theory identifies three major influences: relationship satisfaction, the costs of leaving, and the quality of available alternatives. Commitment increases when people are satisfied with their relationship and perceive separation as costly. It decreases when attractive alternatives seem readily available. Research indicates that relationship satisfaction is generally a stronger predictor of commitment than either the costs of leaving or the quality of alternatives (Benjamin & Agnew, 2003). This finding is encouraging. Abundance does not automatically undermine relationships. When partners are genuinely satisfied, alternative possibilities often lose much of their appeal. However, when satisfaction declines, the presence of numerous alternatives can make departure seem increasingly attractive.

Coping with Romantic Abundance

“Love all, trust a few, do wrong to none.”—William Shakespeare

One way to cope with romantic abundance is by cultivating greater psychological flexibility. Psychological flexibility, often described as the ability to bend without breaking, is associated with mental health and emotional well-being. It involves adapting to changing circumstances, revising priorities when necessary, and maintaining balance among significant life domains. Individuals who are psychologically flexible also tend to enjoy healthier romantic and family relationships (Kashdan & Rottenberg, 2010).

Yet romantic flexibility should not be confused with continually changing partners. Profound love requires a degree of stability. The challenge is to remain flexible enough to adapt to life's changes without becoming so flexible that commitment itself loses significance.

The principle that more is less in romance refers to the abundance of romantic options that keeps people perpetually choosing. Constant comparison can undermine the sustained investment required for profound love and contribute to frustration, loneliness, and uncertainty. The complementary principle that less is more suggests that limiting one's focus to fewer romantic possibilities may create greater depth and meaning. In this sense, fewer alternatives may be associated with greater romantic quality and profundity.

Of course, concepts such as "more" and "less" are context-dependent. As Aristotle observed, what matters is not quantity alone but appropriateness. The challenge of modern romance is therefore not to eliminate abundance, but to find a wise balance within it.

Concluding Thoughts

“Humans die from a lack of love, not a lack of sex.”—Margaret Atwood

Borrowing Charles Dickens's description of the French Revolution, we might say that these are simultaneously "the best of times" and "the worst of times" for lovers. Many relationships are fragile, some are disintegrating, and tempting alternatives are everywhere. Yet these are also flourishing times for love. Love occupies an increasingly central place in people's lives and has become a major standard for evaluating intimate relationships. Romantic love can no longer be easily dismissed as a naive fantasy; for many, it is both a realistic and attainable aspiration.

The paradox is that romantic abundance gives us more opportunities to find love while making it harder to remain deeply invested in it. More choices expand the romantic marketplace, but profound love requires something that abundance often discourages: choosing one person and investing deeply enough to discover what that choice can become.

item.title: Taking My Own Advice About Hobbies
item.description:
Aging

Taking My Own Advice About Hobbies

A psychiatrist tries painting and salsa, and learns when to persist or let go.

Posted October 10, 2026

Key points
  • Hobbies are linked to better mood, life satisfaction, and brain health, even when we are not good at them.
  • Early awkwardness often reflects being a beginner, not a poor fit.
  • Connection, curiosity, and pleasure are all valid reasons to keep going.
  • A time-limited trial with a review date can make the decision to continue or quit more deliberate.

As mental health professionals, we all know the value of hobbies. We recommend them to patients who are stressed, isolated, depressed, or overcoming addiction, and more. Yet until recently, I explored very few, despite giving that advice to others for years. As a workaholic, I often filled my free time with more work and then added volunteer work. I found it extremely rewarding and never felt like I was missing out on anything.

But now, as my friends are starting to retire and are excited to lean into their many hobbies, I decided I'd better find some additional interests. It is a work in progress, and I hope that by sharing a few personal observations, we can learn together. I do enjoy writing. Could that be called a hobby instead of work?

Two Hobbies, Two Very Different Experiences

I have been painting for two years, and I still do not like my work. That is an unfortunate admission. I love art. I have discovered that admiring a beautiful painting and creating one are very different experiences. Two years in, I find myself asking: Why am I doing this? Should I keep going? How long should I give something before being able to create something I love? Are the benefits worth the effort? I really don’t know. I do feel the lessons have improved my writing skills. I enjoy the time I am doing it, and I appreciate the connection with my teacher. My visual skills have heightened but I am tired of giving away/throwing away canvases.

So I decided to try a new hobby and joined a neighbor at a group salsa class. Dancing began even more awkwardly than my attempts at painting. I attended a weekly group class, and for the first few lessons, I felt overwhelmed with anxiety. Then I started taking private lessons and the whole experience changed. Within a month, something shifted: It became fun.

The contrast has made me think about a question many of us face, and one our patients bring to us too: How do we decide which extracurricular pursuits deserve our time, attention, and money?

As a physician, I try to stick with things and strive for mastery. But time and energy are finite. If we stay with everything we start, we leave little room to discover something we might enjoy more. On the other hand, if we leave at the earliest signs of difficulty, we may be missing the opportunity for substantial growth.

Know What You Want From It

Before judging a hobby, it helps to explore your motivation. Are we seeking mastery, relaxation, exercise, connection, or a finished project?

Each goal calls for a different measure of success. A painting can disappoint while the afternoon spent creating it still has value. A dance lesson can be enjoyable long before we have become skilled.

Why Hobbies Matter

There are many good reasons to keep a hobby, and skill is only one of them.

  • Mood and well-being. A 2023 study in Nature Medicine examined data from 93,263 adults aged 65 and older across 16 countries. Having a hobby was associated with fewer depressive symptoms and greater happiness and life satisfaction.[1] Because the study was observational, it cannot prove that hobbies caused these benefits, and nothing in it suggested that becoming accomplished was necessary to experience them.

  • Brain health. Learning something new asks the brain to work in unfamiliar ways: attending, remembering, coordinating, and adjusting. In a study of older adults in the Bronx, Joe Verghese and colleagues found that frequent participation in cognitively engaging leisure activities, such as reading, playing board games, and playing a musical instrument, was associated with a lower risk of dementia. Among the physical activities studied, dancing was the one linked to reduced risk.[2] The 2024 Lancet Commission on dementia also counts physical inactivity and social isolation among the modifiable risk factors for dementia.[3] These are associations, not guarantees, but they suggest that the effort of being a beginner may itself be part of the benefit.

  • Connection. Many hobbies bring us into regular contact with other people. My dance classes have given me something painting has not: a room full of people learning alongside me and laughing at the same missteps. The group usually goes to dinner after class. Social connection matters for health. A meta-analysis of 148 studies found that people with stronger social relationships had a 50 percent greater likelihood of survival over the study periods.[4] A hobby that adds friendly, regular contact to our week may be worth continuing even when progress is slow.

Being a Beginner Is Not the Same as Being a Poor Fit

My experience with dancing reminds me that our first attempts may tell us more about being a beginner than about whether an activity suits us.

Still, time alone does not guarantee progress. Practice needs to offer chances to learn, receive feedback, and try again. A 2014 meta-analysis found that deliberate practice explained 21 percent of the differences in musical performance and 18 percent in sports performance.[5] Those figures describe variation among people, not how much any one person will improve. Practice matters, but much about performance remains unexplained.

The practical lesson is to examine how we are learning before concluding that we lack ability. Would a different teacher help? Are we attempting tasks beyond our current level? Would a smaller, specific goal make progress easier to see? For me, that might mean practicing color mixing or composition, rather than expecting every canvas to be something I want to hang.

Try a Time-Limited Experiment

Research offers no universal deadline for deciding whether to quit a hobby. The activity, our goals, the instruction, and the time available all matter.

One practical approach is a manageable trial: perhaps six to eight weeks of regular participation, with a review date and a budget. This is a suggested experiment, not a scientifically validated cutoff. A complex skill may need much longer; an expensive or physically demanding activity may call for an earlier check-in.

Choose a schedule you can sustain. Twice-weekly private dance lessons work for me right now, but may not be sustainable over the long run. Once I feel some mastery, I look forward to enjoying the group with the added benefit of social connection.

After each session, reflect on the following: Did I enjoy any part of it? Did I learn something? How did I feel afterward? Do I want to return? Then look for a pattern across several sessions. One discouraging afternoon should not decide the future of an interest.

Signs It May Be Worth Continuing

Consider continuing when curiosity survives frustration, when you notice small gains, or when the activity brings connection, satisfaction, or relief from daily demands.

Notice how you feel afterward. You may dread looking awkward beforehand but leave glad you went.

Ask yourself: If no one ever saw the result, would I still want the experience? If the answer is yes, you may need lower expectations rather than a new hobby. We are allowed to be ordinary at something we enjoy.

Signs It May Be Time to Let Go

Consider stopping when repeated participation brings little interest or satisfaction, when the costs outweigh the benefits, or when you continue mainly because you would feel ashamed to quit.

The sunk-cost effect can keep us invested because we have already spent money, effort, or time, or maybe even formed a relationship with a teacher or group.[6] But yesterday's investment does not determine whether next month's lessons are worthwhile. A better question is: Knowing what I know now, would I choose to spend the next few weeks on this?

Research by Carsten Wrosch and colleagues found that the ability to disengage from unattainable goals and commit to new ones was associated with better well-being.[7] That research does not tell us which hobby to leave, but it does challenge the idea that persistence is always the healthiest response.

There are also options between carrying on unchanged and quitting altogether: change teachers, simplify the goal, reduce the frequency, or take a break.

A Note for Clinicians

When a patient wants to stop an activity, it matters why. Someone who fears embarrassment may benefit from smaller steps and support. Someone whose priorities have changed may benefit from permission to move on.

Depression adds another consideration. Reduced pleasure across many activities may reflect anhedonia rather than a poor choice of hobby. Behavioral activation, a structured treatment that helps people re-engage with meaningful activities, has evidence supporting its use for depression; a 2020 Cochrane review included 53 studies with 5,495 participants, though confidence in the findings varied.[8] This is evidence for a broader treatment, but not proof that any particular hobby will help.

We can ask about pleasure, meaning, connection, and accomplishment, while also considering symptoms, practical barriers, and the patient's own values. The goal is to help people make an informed choice about where to put their energy.

Where I Am, for Now

I am still deciding what place painting will have in my life. Dancing has become fun, and it has brought me new people and a new kind of challenge, which makes it easy to return. Neither experience requires a verdict on my talent or character.

We can give ourselves and our patients permission to try something new. To keep going or to let go. The list of possible hobbies is long and the key to success is to find something you love doing.

My best advice: Try something. I am sorry it took me so long to branch out and am grateful for all the new experiences.

item.title: Which Belief Would You Find Unbearable to Revise?
item.description:
Motivated Reasoning

Which Belief Would You Find Unbearable to Revise?

Why our cherished convictions resist scrutiny, and how to question them anyway.

Posted October 10, 2026

Key points
  • Sacred beliefs aren’t just religious; everyday beliefs become sacred when we refuse to question them.
  • Motivated reasoning keeps us holding beliefs by filtering out contrary evidence.
  • Our favored theories are tied to identity, so challenging them can feel like a personal threat.
  • Test a cherished belief: Ask what evidence would change your mind and if an idea is wrong or just threatening.
Source: ChatGPT AI image

When we hear the concept of “sacred belief,” we naturally think of religion. Yet moral psychology shows that everyday beliefs can be sacred as well. A belief becomes sacred when a person refuses to question it due to deep emotional investment and a strong sense of personal and group identity built around it.

The psychological machinery behind sacred beliefs is motivated reasoning. We hold on to a belief, regardless of its empirical defensibility, by filtering out contrary evidence, consciously or otherwise. The antidote is simple to state but difficult to practice: critically interrogating precisely those beliefs we hold most dear. Doing so is essential to epistemic humility, something I learned the hard way.

Despite the title of my blog, I wasn’t always “post-tribal.” I spent my young adult life identifying avidly with the progressive left. I worked for labor unions and community organizations, and had a few jail stints, one in Mexico, for getting into “good trouble.” Years of activism prolonged my Ph.D., and the low pay of social justice work left me paying off college loans into my 40s.

My passion for social justice arose from compassion, anger, and guilt over the world’s stark inequalities. In my sociology courses, I came to see these inequalities as products of history and power relations, a legacy I had unwittingly benefited from simply by being born white and male in a wealthy nation. Years later, I recognized that my embrace of progressive explanations stemmed less from their accuracy than from how deeply they resonated with my emotions and identity.

Mexico, 2000: That's me, an idealistic graduate student, feet-shackled and arrested for supporting a workers' strike.
Source: German Garcia/The Monitor, McAllen, Texas

Here are a few of the sacred beliefs of my youth:

  • Apart from geography and luck, nothing intrinsic to Western culture or institutions explains their success. Western wealth came from stolen resources, continuing today through exploitative global arrangements.
  • The United States is not remotely a meritocracy. Ability and effort are trivial for social mobility, which depends decisively on family resources and connections.
  • Gender inequality endures due to centuries of exclusion by men; any observable differences between men and women in ambition, aggression, nurturance, and career choice are due strictly to socialization, not biology.

I now see these views as one-sided: partially accurate, but not the whole story. I began to change my mind only after identifying the emotional and social needs these beliefs fulfilled for me. Then I started asking myself some questions. Might certain features of Western institutions contribute to their success, but not necessarily translate to other cultures? Might differences in ability matter much more for social mobility than I had assumed? And might average psychological differences between men and women influence their occupational and other choices?

I don’t have settled positions on these questions. But they warrant open discussion, not impassioned dismissal.

How my worldview cracked

The first crack came years ago from an anthropology colleague who challenged my tabula rasa outlook on gender. “Are there any known societies where men’s chastity is rigorously safeguarded while women are encouraged to be sexually libertine?” he would ask. Or: “Can you name any society without sexual jealousy or male concern for paternity?” I had no answer. (“Didn’t Margaret Mead prove something like that?” I wondered.) Steeped in Marxist and feminist theory, I took a purely structural view of behavior, seeing people as marionettes enacting cultural scripts.

The second crack came from the reactions I encountered when I began exploring evolutionary psychology. For most sociologists, evolutionary theories are little more than rationalizations for capitalism and patriarchy. Yet as the chasm widened between my colleagues' zealous opposition and the evidence-based arguments I was reading, I was forced to confront my own motivated reasoning. It was painful. Pursuing a fuller picture of human nature alienated me from valued scholarly networks. Yet in that pain I learned a lesson: Our preferred theories are often far more than analytic tools; they are deeply integrated into our sense of self and how we find meaning in the world.

I recently saw this dynamic play out over lunch. My colleagues and I were discussing the Vanderbilt Report, which argues that left-wing bias is eroding objective research and standards in the humanities and social sciences. A skeptical colleague asked for an example. I offered gender inequality in work roles: “Sociologists emphasize socialization and sexism as key factors shaping the occupational landscape,” I stressed. “But is it plausible that women and men also have, on average, psychological differences that play a role in nudging them toward different career paths?” I saw her hands clench tightly. “I don’t agree with that biology stuff,” she snapped.

I recognized my colleague’s knee-jerk stance, as I once held it myself. The speed and heat of her response suggested a belief being defended rather than examined.

Readers may suspect that my story is another trite example of a liberal coming to embrace conservatism in his later life. Yet my views refuse to align neatly with any political team. I remain as troubled by climate change as I am by the erosion of meritocratic principles in our institutions. My only commitment now is to put truth over tribe.

None of us is immune to motivated reasoning. So what can we do?

Three habits that may help open our minds

  1. Ask what evidence could change your mind. If the honest answer is “none,” you have found a sacred belief.
  2. Notice your body. Clenched hands, a flash of anger, or a sudden urge to change the subject can signal a sacred belief under threat. They can also signal ordinary irritation or a good reason to disagree, so treat them as a cue to look closer, not a verdict.
  3. Separate “this is wrong” from “this is threatening.” Entertaining a hypothesis is not endorsing it.

Epistemic humility is uncomfortable. But if we aim to find the truth, we must be open to being wrong. So ask yourself which belief you would find unbearable to revise. That’s probably the one to examine first.

item.title: How AI Is Influencing Language and Meaning
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

How AI Is Influencing Language and Meaning

As AI-speak assimilates common psychological terms, meanings shift.

Posted October 10, 2026

Key points
  • The emerging AI language is a dynamic system.
  • This evolution of language is altering the meaning and use of words.
  • The term "superintelligence" is an effort to amplify and humanize artificial intelligence.
Psychology permeates all media.
Source: Luskin International, with permission

AI-speak is affecting emotional reactions, stimulating societal shifts and triggering cultural changes. The emerging AI language is a dynamic system in which technical, innovative, emotional, and cultural communication features converge. This evolution of language is altering the meaning and use of many words and creating neologisms and new word formations that shape our communications. Over the past few decades, the tech world has brought many new words and concepts to the language:

  • Crowdsourcing: obtaining contributions from a large group, often via AI online platforms.
  • Google (as a verb): the use of an online search engine as a basis for looking up information on the World Wide Web.
  • Troll: an individual who posts inflammatory, rude, and obnoxious comments online.
  • Bot: a software application that runs automated tasks. Social bots, for example, are human simulations comprised of sets of algorithms that take on repetitive communication tasks.
  • Swarm: a group of controlled or uncontrolled agents. In AI-speak, a swarm of drones is also an example of a swarm of bots.
  • Hashtag: a word or phrase preceded by the symbol # to categorize an item.
  • Superintelligence: a term that attempts to amplify and humanize artificial intelligence. AI has been preceded by evolving terms such as machine learning and data processing as descriptors.

The constant stream of new and hybrid semantics is composed of a blending of technical and emotional language. This formation of words and metaphors supposedly makes tech, and by extension, AI more relatable and easier to understand. Similarly, applying theories in psychology to digital technology helps enhance and enable better communication. In short, AI is triggering language changes, and we need to change our understanding with them.

The following 10 common media psychology terms are being assimilated into AI-speak:

  1. Attention – The study of focus, concentration, and how media captures and sustains attention.
  2. Addiction – The compulsive, often difficult-to-control urge to engage with media content, whether positive or negative.
  3. Emotion – Understanding feelings, moods, and emotional responses triggered by media.
  4. Empathy – The ability to understand and share the feelings of others, often shaped by media representation.
  5. Persuasion – How media messages influence attitudes, beliefs, and behaviors.
  6. Social Identity – How media shapes self-concept and group membership.
  7. Self-Efficacy – Media’s role in influencing confidence and belief in one’s abilities.
  8. Cognitive Load – How media design affects mental processing and learning.
  9. Media Effects – The broader study of how media content and exposure impact cognition, affect, and behavior.
  10. Cultural Influence – How media reflects and shapes cultural norms and values.

While it is important to advance the technology of AI, it's also imperative to be aware of and understand its behavioral and social influences through language that conveys meaning. The technology has no feelings. It is the human response that drives the technology and human behaviors. Simply stated, technology drives the how, and media and communications psychology explains the why. The challenge in effective communication involves this continuous search for meaning.

Another influential language criterion requires an understanding of de facto standards. A de facto standard occurs when a group of users follows a guideline. Words can have precise meanings and established boundaries. There are thousands of for-profit and nonprofit associations advocating points of view and/or assigning competence in compliance. The thousands of associations influence language, advocate meaning, and promote de facto standards. De facto standards are not necessarily in law, but they do substantially influence individuals as well as commerce. AI influences each professional association. Therefore, voluntary cooperation in the establishment of de facto standards is an imperative for effective, clear, and precise communication.

In my opinion, Congress can effectively adopt both legal and recommended guidelines for AI in efforts to maintain safety and contribute productive results. Associations, as major contributors to culture and our economy, are key in identifying specific issues and can apply useful nongovernmental guidelines to people and products. We live in a world of de facto standards as well as formalized laws enforceable by government through our legal system, and this forms the basis of language literacy.

Media literacy offers a safeguard against misinformation and is a tool of informed citizenship. Major universities are leading the way in fostering media literacy: Emerson College offers a degree program in Media Psychology, Stanford University offers a program in Media and Communications Psychology, and MIT's Comparative Media Studies program is another good example among the many programs that address the social, cultural, political, and ethical implications of media literacy. It is now time to follow the leaders in facilitating wide-scale media literacy.

Schools, colleges, and universities should all consider giving increased attention to media literacy. In AI, technology is the engine, media psychology is the rudder, and media literacy is the outcome. Public and professional understanding is the goal.

In 1986, the American Psychological Association established its Media Psychology Division 46 to study, analyze, and report on the behavioral nexus between psychology and technology. Division 46, also known as the Society for Media Psychology and Technology, can play a leading role in the evolution of the psychological meaning of words between human beings and machines of all types.

This post is a call to action that urges readers to be alert to neologisms and new usages triggered by AI in our continuing search for meaning in language and emphasizes the need for schools, colleges, associations, and the government to work together as the language explaining AI evolves.

item.title: Seven Ways to Understand Loneliness in the Age of AI
item.description:
Loneliness

Seven Ways to Understand Loneliness in the Age of AI

A new review maps why we feel disconnected, as AI begins to reshape belonging.

Posted October 10, 2026

Key points
  • Loneliness is a felt gap between the connection we want and what we have, not how many people we know.
  • Seven theories, from attachment to evolution, frame loneliness as a signal, an absence, or lost belonging.
  • Rejection sensitivity, low trust, and negative self-evaluation can make disconnection self-reinforcing.
  • AI may drive a K-shaped split: some retreat into AI companionship, while others seek human connection.

We are reminded daily of the terrible harms loneliness can inflict on the human mind, body, and brain—and on the very texture of the social fabric (Holt-Lunstad, 2024; World Health Organization, 2025). Large language models, which are mind-like and designed to capitalize on human tendencies toward communication and relationship in order to drive use, and revenue, may offer companionship to people who need company.

At the same time that AI may assuage loneliness—and, used with intention, help bring people together—contemporary use is not so safeguarded, running the risk of damaging the “connective tissue” that holds humanity together. That connective tissue is already under strain from social media, the aftermath of pandemic-related isolation (especially for developing minds and communities), geopolitical upheaval and intergroup conflict, and the sheer mass of a humanity now exceeding 8 billion souls. From an individual perspective, each of us is a smaller and smaller fraction of the whole.

Understanding how social connection works helps us develop effective ways of combatting loneliness and building connection. One example is social prescribing, pioneered at London’s Bromley by Bow Centre beginning in 1984, in which clinicians refer people to “link workers” who connect them with non-clinical community resources—arts and nature groups, exercise, volunteering, housing and employment support. England’s National Health Service adopted the model nationally in 2019 (Chikwira, 2026).

Loneliness is a multidimensional experience: an imbalance between the people we want to connect with and those who are available, or perceived to be available. A recent review in the Journal of Social Patterns & Perspectives (Hoque, 2026) synthesizes this literature, identifying seven theoretical perspectives, six psychological mechanisms, and six features of today’s social environment.

Seven Perspectives on Loneliness and Connectedness

The multidimensional view. Anchored in the subjective experience of relationship deficit, this view emphasizes one’s sense of not having enough social ties—regardless of how many friends one has—and the quality of connection over sheer quantity.

Emotional absence. Loneliness is perceived as “relational absence,” missing or lost connection. The remedy is meaningful, valued attachment.

The life-course perspective. Social needs change across development, so ways of addressing loneliness need to take stage of life into account. Different groups carry different risks, and call for different strategies.

Evolutionary theory. Loneliness is an “adaptive social signal” requiring response, much like hunger or pain. Being cut off from others draws attention to the problem and, when effective, motivates restoring or creating connection—though chronic activation can tip toward vigilance and withdrawal instead (Cacioppo & Cacioppo, 2018).

Belongingness. People need relationships, and perceived belonging is critical to mental and physical health. Restoring belonging, through individual and community efforts, is needed for people to be well, and flourish.

Attachment theory. We are born requiring relationships for safety and security. Secure attachment supports healthy development, while insecure attachment is associated with a range of negative outcomes, including difficulty with closeness.

Social identity theory. Our social identities hold us and add a layer of meaning, undergirding belonging while providing shared purpose and opportunities to collaborate. Not identifying with any group diminishes the sense of belonging.

Six Psychological Mechanisms

Social reward processing. How we value social interaction drives approach or avoidance. Rewarding social situations support building and maintaining relationships.

Social cognition. How we interpret social cues shapes whether we feel a sense of affiliation, and so whether we seek others out or avoid them.

Rejection sensitivity. How painful rejection feels affects whether we keep pursuing relationships given the perceived risk. Social exclusion activates brain regions overlapping with those involved in physical pain (Eisenberger et al., 2003).

Emotion regulation. How we manage social distress determines whether we respond to loneliness adaptively or maladaptively.

Self-evaluation. Seeing ourselves more positively supports self-confidence, which protects against isolation by easing the path to social engagement.

Interpersonal trust. When trust is lower—a result of life experience, upbringing, and temperament—mutual interdependence is undermined. Exaggerated self-reliance is often a factor, leading to avoidance of healthy dependence and reduced cooperation. Trust is required for stable relationships to flourish.

How Today’s Environments Shape Connection

The review identifies six contemporary factors, each cutting both ways.

Social media maintains distant ties but can increase perceived disconnection.

Digital comparison, seeing so many others who appear better off, can worsen self-evaluation, yet online spaces also offer avenues for support.

Hybrid work offers flexibility but can reduce workplace belonging.

Urban mobility opens new social opportunities while undermining durable relationships.

Family and friendship networks strengthen connectedness when strong, but not everyone has equal access to them.

Digital interaction expands social access, though the relationships it supports are, on average, different from—and often thinner than—in-person ones.

Future Directions

Loneliness has been called an epidemic, with health effects that popular accounts liken to smoking up to 15 cigarettes a day (Holt-Lunstad et al., 2010; Office of the U.S. Surgeon General, 2023), and has been declared a public health priority by authorities including the U.S. Surgeon General and the World Health Organization. Initiatives are underway on many fronts. The review closes with a multilevel framework (below), moving from psychological, relational, and social understanding toward community-based, digital, and population-sensitive interventions, and calling for longitudinal, cross-cultural, and comparative research.

Given the surge in artificial intelligence, not strongly discussed in the review, we can expect the landscape of loneliness and social connection to shift in ways hard to predict, with both benefit and harm. We may see a “K-shaped” response, where AI leads some to greater isolation as agents become primary attachment objects, while others are driven to seek human connection. Some may find a balance.

item.title: How to Manage After-School Restraint Collapse
item.description:
Parenting

How to Manage After-School Restraint Collapse

Why does my child fall apart after school?

Posted October 10, 2026

Key points
  • After holding it together all day at school, children may arrive home exhausted and frustrated.
  • Children may save their behavioral outbursts for home because that's where they feel safe.
  • It's important to understand their behavior, but do not excuse it.
  • Your child needs connection, not confrontation.

Let’s set the scene. You watch your child walk through the door after getting home from school. You smile and ask, “How was your day?” Imagine your surprise when your child responds, “FINE!” or “Just leave me alone!” You back off, but their younger sibling tries to give them a hug, which they resist. And suddenly... your sweet child is unrecognizable. There are tears. There's yelling. They tell you they hate you. They run to their bedroom and slam the door.

You are dumbfounded. You reach out to your child’s teacher only to find out that their behavior at school was perfect, as usual. And you're standing there thinking: What happened to my child? Sound familiar? This is called after-school restraint collapse. This term was developed by Andrea Loewen Nair, a psychotherapist and parenting educator. After-school restraint collapse explains a child who copes well emotionally during school, but when they get home, things get ugly. The child releases their stress and frustration in a dramatic manner. They may throw a temper tantrum, shut down, break objects around the house, or laugh uncontrollably.

This is a difficult situation. Yet your child is not intentionally saving their worst behavior for you. On the contrary. They may finally let go and release their emotions because home is the place where they finally feel safe enough to stop holding everything together. And that distinction matters.

After-school restraint collapse has received quite a bit of attention recently, but the underlying concept isn't new. It is important to note that after-school restraint collapse is not a medical diagnosis. It is simply a term to describe a pattern of behavior. Children do not have fully developed brains. Their capacity to manage stress, regulate their emotions, and express appropriate behavior can vary tremendously. There is only so much they can take within a given day.

View your child's ability to regulate themselves physically, mentally, and emotionally as a battery. They wake up with a defined amount of battery life. Then they go to school, where there are rules and expectations. Think about everything that is asked during a typical school day. Sit in your seat. Listen. Complete your work. Wait in line. Raise your hand before talking. Don't interrupt. Transition to another activity seamlessly. Ignore the kid who is distracting you. Get on the bus. Manage frustration without distracting other students. Each task, each expectation slowly drains the battery.

When your child gets home, that emotional battery may be at 1 percent. And then you say, "How was your day? or “Do you have any homework?” And then everything falls apart. Cue the tantrum. The yelling. The slamming of doors or destruction of property.

Your child’s undesired after-school behavior indicates: “I kept it together all day. I’m spent." That does not mean children are allowed to be disrespectful or hurtful, or to break things around the house. Understanding behavior is not the same thing as allowing the behavior, and that's an important distinction. We can enforce, "I understand why this is hard for you, and I'm still going to provide effective discipline."

If after-school restraint collapse is happening regularly in your home, I want you to experiment with the following five steps:

  • Connect
  • Refuel
  • Validate
  • Reduce demands
  • Reconnect

Step one is to connect. When your child gets home from school, simply smile at them. Say "I'm happy to see you." Offer a hug. Resist the urge to ask them questions about their day, at least initially.

Step two is to refuel, physically and emotionally. Offer your child a snack. Give them time and space to decompress, even if that means using an electronic device.

Step three is to validate their emotions. Read their body language. If they seem upset, say something to the effect of, “You seem angry. Do you want to talk about it?” Or, “You seem really happy. I’d love to hear why.”

Step four is to temporarily reduce demands. After school, children need a transition period. Try saying, “Welcome home. Do you need anything from me?” Provide time and space for your child to self-regulate, physically and emotionally. Maybe your child needs to read for 15 minutes. Or jump on a trampoline. Or cuddle with their dog.

Step five is to reconnect and remind them of the tasks at hand. This is important, as it reinforces the concept that children have expectations that need to be met. Homework needs to be completed. The backpack needs to be packed and put away. Teeth need to be brushed, and baths or showers need to be taken.

Behavior is a form of communication. Pay attention to the patterns because patterns of behavior are powerful. Don't judge. Collect data. You might discover: “Yikes. Wednesdays are challenging because band practice starts at 7:30 a.m. and softball practice is from 5:30 to 7:30 p.m. Or, "The days she doesn't eat much at lunch are consistently harder." Or, "He does much better when he has 30 minutes of downtime before starting homework. Now you're not guessing. You're learning your child.

Greeting your child after school does not need to lead to an emotional meltdown. You can connect with your child without fueling a meltdown.

item.title: 4 Reasons to Trade TikTok for a Feature Film
item.description:
Social Media

4 Reasons to Trade TikTok for a Feature Film

Why one long story may do more for your mind than a thousand short ones.

Posted October 10, 2026

Key points
  • A review of 71 studies links heavy short-form video use to poorer attention, mood, and sleep.
  • How intensely you engage with short videos may matter more than how often you open the app.
  • Getting absorbed in one long story may help you practice sustained focus and see new perspectives.
  • Watching a film with others can build social bonds, while endless solo scrolling is tied to loneliness.

In a 2025 synthesis of 71 studies, the researchers confirmed both new and previously known insights into the negative effects of engagement with short-form video content for three or more hours per day, including compulsive use, poorer cognitive and mental health, body image issues, social isolation, feelings of loneliness, anger, lower self-esteem, and reduced life satisfaction.

Short video consumption affects everyone with a smartphone—all ages, all genders, all over the world. For many people, short-form video content is their main source of entertainment, news, information, and engagement outside of school, friends, family, and work.

Based on their discussion and conclusions, below are four reasons why putting down the phone and watching a feature film may be a good alternative. If you are already spending three hours each day on 15-second videos, you can replace that time with a single movie and avoid the negative effects associated with excessive short-form video consumption.

  1. The fast, unpredictable rewards of short videos can reinforce compulsive use. Instead, try watching one film and become transported into the story. Being absorbed in a film helps individuals process emotions more deeply and become aware of new perspectives.
  2. Named the Oxford English Dictionary’s 2024 Word of the Year, brain rot is “a perceived loss of intelligence or critical thinking skills, esp. (in later use) as attributed to the overconsumption of unchallenging or inane content or material” such as some of the negative effects linked to endlessly scrolling short videos on TikTok, Instagram Reels, or YouTube Shorts. Engagement with TikTok is linked to poorer cognitive and mental health across all ages. A higher frequency does not necessarily affect mood or cognition, but the intensity of one’s engagement does. The more intensely one watches, the more there is a decrease in one’s attention span and an increase in depression, anxiety, stress, loneliness, and poorer sleep quality. A 120-minute film, for instance, lets your brain follow one story rather than a new one every 15 seconds, and practicing focus tends to strengthen one’s focus.
  3. Self-esteem around body image largely depends on the short-form content someone is consuming in isolation, where they begin to compare themselves to unrealistic beauty standards. However, watching a film with others lets you bond over the content. It also allows you to reality-check the content you are watching so you do not just internalize the negativity. The social side of watching films is beneficial because it brings you together with others, while infinite scrolling is linked to increased social isolation and loneliness.
  4. Excessive TikTok use (3+ hours per day) is also associated with increased anger, lower self-esteem, and reduced life satisfaction. A film gives you two hours inside someone else’s life, long enough to understand their choices and contradictions. One may even develop empathy by watching and feeling what another person experiences in a feature-length, story-based film.

Five films that are recommended viewing for maximum absorption, less screen time, and building new perspectives:

A Beautiful Mind
Source: Universal Pictures and DreamWorks Pictures

A Beautiful Mind (2001): Ron Howard beautifully portrays mathematician John Nash. One is immediately pulled into his reality, and when the truth about his schizophrenia is revealed, you share and can empathize with his disorientation and come away with a new understanding of living with mental illness.

Schindler's List
Source: Universal Pictures

Schindler’s List (1993): Steven Spielberg’s black-and-white Holocaust drama feels like history unfolding in real time, holding your full attention on one man’s moral awakening and the lives he saved. You will have a hard time looking at your phone during this film.

Saving Private Ryan (1998): Steven Spielberg’s WWII epic drops you onto Omaha Beach within its first 25 minutes, turning a single rescue mission into a reckoning with sacrifice, duty, and what we owe each other. One of the best narrative films to fall into for 2 hours and 49 minutes.

Lord of the Rings
Source: Warner Bros.

The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring (2001): This film is the ultimate immersive fantasy, drawing you into the tactile, lived-in world of Middle-earth from its opening Shire scenes and into one story about friendship that lasts 3+ hours.

Spirited Away
Source: Studio Ghibli

Spirited Away (2001): Step through a tunnel and into Hayao Miyazaki’s hand-drawn spirit world, where every frame is something strange and wondrous. Studio Ghibli utilizes fluid character motion, hand-drawn beauty, and striking color contrasts, making the environment feel like a living painting. It is a pleasure for your mind and your eyes.
